Introduction¶

In this project, we will investigate which audio features of a song can be used to predict a song's popularity. Below is a table of all the features included in the data set.

Feature Description Range / Unit
Popularity Spotify popularity score 0–100
Danceability Suitability for dancing 0–1
Energy Intensity and activity of the track 0–1
Loudness Average loudness Decibels (dB)
Speechiness Presence of spoken words 0–1
Acousticness Likelihood that the track is acoustic 0–1
Instrumentalness Likelihood that the track has no vocals 0–1
Liveness Likelihood of a live recording 0–1
Valence Musical positivity or happiness 0–1
Tempo Speed of the track Beats per minute (BPM)
Duration Length of the track Milliseconds
Key Estimated musical key 0–11
Mode Major or minor mode 0 or 1
Time Signature Estimated beats per measure Integer

| Explicitness | Contains explicit lyrics | True/False

For our research question, the features we will use for our analysis include: danceability, energy, loudness, speechiness, acousticness, instrumentalness, liveness, valence, and tempo. Popularity is based off of total number of plays a track has and how recent those plays are. The initial data set has 114000 entries.

data = pd.read_csv('/content/drive/MyDrive/Colab/math237/data/dataset.csv')

Cleaning¶

Before we begin our analysis, we first take out songs with duplicate entries and songs with missing values. There is only one song with missing columns. It has a track ID, but no name, artist, or popularity. Therefore we will remove the song from our data. There are 24,259 songs with duplicate track ID's in our dataset. We will also drop these songs to prevent repeated entries from disproportionately affecting our analysis.

# find rows with missing values
rows_with_nan = data[data.isna().any(axis=1)]
print(rows_with_nan)
# drop missing row and duplicates
my_spot = data.drop(index=rows_with_nan.index)
my_spot = my_spot.drop_duplicates(subset=['track_id']).copy()
# how many songs removed
n_diff = len(data) - len(my_spot)
print(f'Removed {n_diff} songs.')

Aside from missing data and duplicate ID's, we noticed that there was a high amount songs with a popularity score of 0,1, and 2. There are two explanations for this. The first is that these songs were recently uploaded to spotify at the time of data collection and have not had the time to gather plays. The second is because some songs show up multiple times, yet have different track ID's. This is because they are apart of "collection albums," which are essentially a playlist of songs that are under the same category. The songs in these albums tend to have a much lower score than the song uploaded by the original artist, so we remove them from the data to get a better estimation of our features.

Initial Statistics¶

Now that we have cleaned the data, we can start the initial analysis of our dataset. Across the entire dataset, the mean popularity is 37.823 with a standard deviation of 17.573. From the histogram, we can see that the popularity of songs is somewhat normally distributed across the range of 0-100.

#histogram with popularity on x-axis and amount on y-axis
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.hist(my_spot['popularity'], bins=15, color='skyblue', alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black')
plt.title('Distribution of Popularity', fontsize=16)
plt.xlabel('Popularity', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Number of songs', fontsize=12)
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

Most and Least Popular Artists¶

The summary tables were created using Pandas grouping and aggregation functions to calculate average popularity and song counts for artists and genres with at least 10 songs in the deduplicated dataset. Filtering by a 10 track minimum isolates established performers and prominent genres to prevent single track outliers from skewing the results.

Based on the 'Top 10 Most Popular Artists and Genres' data, Bad Bunny leads all artists with an average popularity score of 85.36 across 22 songs, followed by Travis Scott (74.93), Frank Ocean (74.71), The Neighbourhood (73.92), and Radiohead (73.55). For genres, k pop ranks highest with an average popularity of 59.36 across 917 songs, closely followed by pop film (59.10) and metal (56.42), with chill (53.74) and latino (51.79) also in the top tier.

The output shows clear listener preference for modern pop, rap, rock, and the global music genres. While top individual artists can average popularity scores above 80, genre averages cap under 60 because they incorporate hundreds of tracks with varying performance levels across Spotify.

# Popularity of artists with at least 10 rated songs
artist_stats = my_spot.groupby('artists').agg(
    avg_popularity=('popularity', 'mean'),
    song_count=('popularity', 'count')
).reset_index()

popular_artists = artist_stats[artist_stats['song_count'] >= 10].sort_values(by='avg_popularity', ascending=False)

top_5_artists = popular_artists.head(10)
print("Top 10 Most Popular Artists (on average, with at least 10 songs):")
display(top_5_artists)

The summary table was created using Pandas grouping, aggregation, and filtering to calculate average popularity scores and song counts for artists with at least 20 songs. Setting a 20-track minimum isolates established acts, ensuring small catalog drops don't skew the results.

Based on the "5 Least Popular Artists (on average, with at least 20 songs)" output, Farzad Golpayegani records the lowest average popularity score at 3.90 across 20 songs. He is followed by Aril Brikha (7.58), Surgeon (7.71), Model 500 (8.14), and Ron Trent (8.76), with Octave One, Alphaxone, Underground Resistance, Crows in the Rain, and Theo Parrish rounding out the bottom ten.

These low scores reflect the niche subgenres these artists operate in—such as underground techno, deep house, ambient, and avant-garde music. Unlike mainstream pop or rap acts designed for mass radio play and viral playlisting, these performers cater to specialized subcultures and deep-catalog collectors, resulting in lower overall streaming scores on Spotify.

Explicit vs. Non-Explicit¶

The bar plot displays the explicitness of all songs within the data set (not including duplicates) and compares it with their average popularity. The x-axis represents all of the songs, whether they are explicit or clean, and the y-axis represents average popularity. It achieves this by averaging all the popularity scores for all explicit songs and non-explicit songs and comparing them. As shown, there is little to no difference on if the popularity of a song correlates with if it is explicit or not. However explicit songs take a slight edge with a higher score of 4.5 average popularity.

Song Duration¶

The histogram was created using Matplotlib's plt.hist() function with 2,000 bins to visualize the distribution of track lengths across the entire dataset. By converting track duration from milliseconds to minutes (duration_ms / 60000), the plot provides an intuitive look at how song lengths are distributed.

Based on the 'Duration Distribution' graph, the visualization helps identify the common length of songs in the Spotify dataset. Most tracks cluster heavily around the typical 3-to-4-minute mark, creating a sharp central peak. However, because 2000 bins were specified, the distribution reveals fine granularity, including extreme outliers such as ultra-short tracks under a minute and exceptionally long ambient, spoken-word, or classical audio tracks extending well beyond standard song lengths.

The histogram shows how audio track length varies across the dataset. The strong central concentration indicates that most songs adhere to standard commercial track lengths, while the long right tail highlights the presence of non-traditional or genre-specific audio formats. These patterns suggest that while mainstream music heavily favors standard durations, track length alone can vary significantly depending on the specific type of audio content.

my_spot["duration_min"] = my_spot["duration_ms"] / 60000
plt.hist(my_spot['duration_min'], bins = 2000)
plt.title('Duration Distribution')
plt.xlabel('Duration in Minutes')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.xlim(0, 10)
plt.show()

Scatter Plots¶

We plot each audio feature on the x-axis and popularity on the y-axis to visualize the relationship between them. We can use these to identify some pattern across the variables. While its hard to see the correlation between features and popularity, we can see some clusters form in the graphs. In the Speechiness graph, we can see that there is a small cluster of songs that have high speechiness and low popularity.

# plot each audio feature on the x-axis with popularity on the y-axis
audio_features = [
    'danceability', 'energy', 'loudness', 'speechiness',
    'valence', 'liveness', 'instrumentalness', 'acousticness',
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(18, 10))
axes = axes.flatten()

for i, feature in enumerate(audio_features):
    axes[i].scatter(my_spot[feature], my_spot['popularity'], alpha=0.5)
    axes[i].set_xlabel(feature, fontsize=1)
    axes[i].set_ylabel('Popularity', fontsize=1)
    axes[i].set_title(f'{feature} vs. Popularity', fontsize=12)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Correlation Heat Map¶

We use a heatmap to visualize the correlations between each audio feature and popularity. While there are no features that have a high, positive correlation with popularity, we can see that some features have a high, positive correlation with each other. Notably, energy and loudness have a high correlation as well as danceability and valence. However, there are audio features with a negative correlation with positivity, those being instrumentalness and speechiness.

categorical_features = [
    'popularity', 'danceability', 'energy', 'loudness', 'speechiness',
    'valence', 'liveness', 'instrumentalness', 'acousticness',
]



# Calculate the correlation matrix
corr_matrix = my_spot[categorical_features].corr()

# Generate the heatmap
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(
    corr_matrix,
    annot=True,
    cmap='coolwarm',
    fmt='.2f',
    linewidths=0.5,
    vmin=-1,
    vmax=1
)
plt.title('Correlation of Audio Features', fontsize=14, pad=15)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Feature Engineering¶

Apart from cleaning the data, we also decided to split the songs into different bins of based off popularity. This will allow us to further investigate audio features across songs with low, medium, and high popularity. We based our cutoffs on the interquartile range to insure we have a proportionate amount of samples in each bin. The box and whisker plot shows Q1, median and Q3 of the data. To make our bins, we split the data from 0 to 30 since that is half way between Q1 and the median. From there we did the same thing for the median and Q3, giving us 30 to 44 as our second bin, leaving 44 to 100 as our final bin.

my_spot['Pop_level'] = pd.cut(
    my_spot['popularity'],
    bins = [-1,30,44,100],
    labels = ['Low', 'Medium', 'High']
)

# Min-Max normalization formula for loudness
my_spot['loudness_scaled'] = (my_spot['loudness'] - my_spot['loudness'].min()) / (
    my_spot['loudness'].max() - my_spot['loudness'].min()
)
# Min-Max normalization formula for tempo
my_spot['tempo_scaled'] = (my_spot['tempo'] - my_spot['tempo'].min()) / (
    my_spot['tempo'].max() - my_spot['tempo'].min()
)
my_spot['average_score'] = my_spot[['danceability', 'loudness_scaled', 'tempo_scaled']].mean(axis=1)

# 2. Calculate the mean 'average_score' for each popularity bin
bar_data = my_spot.groupby('Pop_level', observed=False)['popularity'].mean()

# 3. Plot it
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
bar_data.plot(kind='bar', color='mediumseagreen', edgecolor='black', width=0.8)

plt.title('Average Audio Score by Popularity Range', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', pad=15)
plt.xlabel('Popularity Range (0-100)', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Mean Average Score (Danceability, Energy, Valence)', fontsize=12)
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Features By Genre¶

Now we compare features across genre. We hypothsized that the high deviations in some features is due to the difference in genre. We looked at the 5 most popular genres and investigated the audio features of what leads to a popular song. We found that the 5 most popular song genres are electro, pop, soul, house, and rock. We can already see the difference in popularity mean across genre compared to the mean of popularity across all songs is high.

# top 5 most popular genres
avg = my_spot.groupby('track_genre')['popularity'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)

We can also see that the standard deviation across features is much lower across genres.

# create new dataframes for top 5 most popular genres
electro = my_spot[my_spot['track_genre'] == 'electro']
rock = my_spot[my_spot['track_genre'] == 'rock']
pop = my_spot[my_spot['track_genre'] == 'pop']
soul = my_spot[my_spot['track_genre'] == 'soul']
house = my_spot[my_spot['track_genre'] == 'house']

# standard deviation for each category
sd_electro = electro[audio_features].std()
sd_rock = rock[audio_features].std()
sd_pop = pop[audio_features].std()
sd_soul = soul[audio_features].std()
sd_house = house[audio_features].std()

# standard deviations for each feature (0 = electro, 1 = rock, 2 = pop, 3 = soul, 4 = house)
print(pd.concat([sd_electro, sd_rock, sd_pop, sd_soul, sd_house], axis=1))

Correlation Heat Maps¶

We will use heat maps to visualize correlation across audio features by genre. We can see that some genres differ in which features correlate with higher popularity. For example, we can see that speechiness has a positive correlation with popularity for soul music, but a negative correlation with popularity for electro music.

# correlation matrix for each genre
corr_matrix_electro = electro[categorical_features].corr()
corr_matrix_rock = rock[categorical_features].corr()
corr_matrix_pop = pop[categorical_features].corr()
corr_matrix_soul = soul[categorical_features].corr()
corr_matrix_house = house[categorical_features].corr()

genres = ['electro', 'pop', 'rock', 'soul', 'house']

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 10))
axes = axes.flatten()

for i, genre in enumerate(genres):
    corr_matrix = globals()[f'corr_matrix_{genre}']

    sns.heatmap(
        corr_matrix,
        annot=True,
        cmap='coolwarm',
        fmt='.2f',
        linewidths=0.5,
        vmin=-1,
        vmax=1,
        ax=axes[i],
        cbar=False
    )

    axes[i].set_title(f'Correlation for {genre}', fontsize=12, pad=10)

# remove unused sixth subplot
fig.delaxes(axes[5])

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Discussion¶

We can separate these music genres into accoustic (soul, pop, rock) and synthesized (house, electro) music. We create these groups to distinguish the fact that different features correlate with higher popularity. A common factor across the accoustic group is that speechiness correlates positively with popularity. We can infer that the presence of lyrics is important for these genres. Accousticness is also a feature that correlates positively with popularity. This highlights the importance of sound created by instruments rather than synthesized music in these genres. For the synthesized group, we can see that the feature is slightly favored is liveness. This means that the songs that are most popular in these genres are songs that were performed live. One interesting thing to note, is that the electro genre's features do not highly correlate with popularity at all. This could be mean that there are some outside factors that drive this genre to popularity, like cultural trends or the artist who composed the song.

Features By Genre with Popularity Bins¶

The bar chart is created using the facet_wrap() function to compare the number of songs across the ten most frequently occurring music genres based on their popularity levels. By separating low, medium, and high levels into their own panels.

Based on the Number of Songs by Genre and Popularity graph, the X-axis represents the different music genres, while the Y-axis represents the number of songs within each popularity category. The songs are classified into three popularity levels. Low is (0-30), Medium (31-44), and High (45-100). In the high-popularity category, club has 229 songs, followed by forro with 219 songs and Disney with 117 songs. In contrast, in the low category, comedy and Chicago have the highest numbers of low-popularity songs, with 922 and 916 songs. As for the medium popularity, forro has the highest number of songs at 779, followed by club with 369 songs. These insights show that the number of songs within each popularity category varies across different music genres.

The visualization shows how song popularity differs across music genres. The bar graph shows club and forro have large numbers of highly popular songs compared with other selected genres, while comedy, Chicago-house, and bluegrass have a large number of songs with low popularity songs. Lastly, forro has a high number of medium-popularity songs, while the rest don't meet half of 779. These differences suggest a possible association between music genre and song popularity. However, because the graph displays song counts rather than percentages, it cannot determine which genres have the highest proportion of popular songs

top_genres = my_spot['track_genre'].value_counts().head(10).index

spotify_top10 = my_spot[my_spot['track_genre'].isin(top_genres)]

(
    ggplot(spotify_top10)
    + geom_bar(aes(x = 'track_genre', fill = 'Pop_level'), position= 'dodge')
    + labs(
        title = 'Numbers of songs by Genre and Popularity',
        x = 'Music Genre',
        y = 'Number of Songs',
        fill = 'Popularity Level'
    )

    + facet_wrap('Pop_level')


)

The grouped bar chart was created to show the relationship between music genre and song popularity by comparing the percentage of songs classified as having low, medium, or high popularity. Unlike the previous graphs that displayed the numbers of songs, this visualization uses percentages to account for differences in the total number of songs within each genre.

Based on the grouped bar chart, the X-axis represents the different music genres, while the Y-axis represents the percentage of songs within each popularity category. The results show that the club has the highest percentage of highly popular songs at 23%, followed by forro at 22%, then Disney at 12%. In contrast, comedy has the highest percentage of songs labeled as low popularity at 93%, followed by chicago at 92%. As for the medium popularity category, forro has the highest percentage at 78%, followed by club at 37%. These findings show the popularity levels are distributed differently across music genres, as some genres have a greater proportion of highly popular songs while others are dominated by low-popularity songs.

The visualization helps answer the genre portion of the research question by showing how the distribution of song popularity differs across music genres. The visualization uses percentages to make comparisons across genres regardless of their total count. These findings show a possible association between music genre and song popularity because the proportion of songs in each popularity category varies across genres.

genre_percent = (
    spotify_top10
    .groupby(['track_genre', 'Pop_level'], observed=True)
    .size()
    .reset_index(name='count')
)

genre_percent['percentage'] = (
    genre_percent['count']
    / genre_percent.groupby('track_genre')['count'].transform('sum')
    * 100
)
(
    ggplot(genre_percent)
    + geom_bar(
      aes(
            x='track_genre',
            y='percentage',
            fill='Pop_level'
        ),
        stat='identity',
        position='dodge'
    )
    +labs(
        title='Percentage of Popularity Levels by Genre',
        x='Music Genre',
        y='Percentage of Songs (%)',
        fill='Popularity Level'
    )
    + scale_y_continuous(
        breaks=[0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100],
        limits=[0, 100]
    )
    + theme(
        axis_text_x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1)
    )
    + ggsize(900, 600)
)

Conclusion¶

This project analyzed a cleaned dataset of 114,000 Spotify tracks to determine which audio features and characteristics best predict a song's popularity. The findings revealed that popularity scores are somewhat normally distributed with an average of 37.8, and that standard commercial track lengths of 3 to 4 minutes heavily dominate the dataset. While factors like explicit content have only a minimal impact on overall success, specific audio profiles yield distinct trends, such as tracks with high "speechiness" consistently clustering alongside lower popularity scores. Ultimately, while individual acoustic features demonstrate complex relationships with track performance, mainstream genres like Electro and Pop, along with established top artists, remain the strongest indicators of high popularity.
